title: Software for multi-omics data integration and analysis: a systematic and critical comparison of frameworks, packages, workflows and platforms, with EasyMultiProfiler as a featured workflow for microbiome research

sections.heading: Introduction: why multi-omics integration demands dedicated software
sections.goal: Establish that the heterogeneity of multi-omics assays, the proliferation of integration algorithms and the reproducibility crisis in computational biology have together created demand for dedicated software stacks. Frame microbiome research as a particularly demanding subdomain because host, microbial, viral and metabolic layers must be coordinated, and motivate a comparative review that uses common criteria rather than enumerating tools. The critical angle: integration is not merely a statistical problem but an engineering and infrastructure problem, and current reviews often conflate algorithms with workflows.

sections.heading: A taxonomy of integration strategies: stages, supervision and biological target
sections.goal: Introduce a working taxonomy that organises the field along three axes: (i) integration stage (early/intermediate/late, corresponding to concatenation, joint embedding and decision-level fusion); (ii) supervision (unsupervised factor analysis, semi-supervised, supervised); and (iii) biological target (subtyping, biomarker selection, longitudinal modelling, dynamic network inference). The critical angle: labels such as 'multi-omics integration' hide very different statistical commitments, and conflating similarity-network fusion with matrix factorisation obscures the assumptions each method imposes on the data.

sections.heading: General-purpose statistical and Bioconductor integration frameworks
sections.goal: Survey general-purpose frameworks that operate on any multi-omics block regardless of biological domain: PLS-based integrative methods, Bayesian factor analysis, the MultiAssayExperiment data class, pathway-level roll-ups and pipelines that wrap multiple algorithms. The critical angle: PLS-based methods (mixOmics and DIABLO) remain popular but assume linear relationships and correlated blocks, while matrix factorisation (MOFA/MOFA+) brings stronger probabilistic grounding yet still requires careful modelling of missingness and modality-specific noise; generalist packages rarely ship microbiome-aware preprocessing.

sections.heading: Microbiome-centred multi-omics tools
sections.goal: Compare tools designed specifically for microbiome multi-omics, where 16S, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and host-response layers must be aligned. Include both dedicated pipelines (gNOMO, gNOMO2) and dynamic-modelling approaches (PALM), as well as domain-bridging efforts for non-model hosts, livestock and clinical microbiome cohorts. The critical angle: microbiome multi-omics suffers from severe annotation bottlenecks, strain-level ambiguity and limited gold-standard benchmarks; very few tools explicitly couple integration with microbiome-specific QC, taxonomic aggregation and pathway mapping, leaving a gap that EasyMultiProfiler attempts to fill.

sections.heading: Web servers and point-and-click platforms for multi-omics
sections.goal: Catalogue browser-based platforms that lower the programming barrier and discuss the trade-off between accessibility and methodological transparency. The critical angle: web platforms accelerate uptake but frequently lag behind algorithmic state-of-the-art, hide preprocessing choices, and offer limited customisation; 'unified' platforms often simply concatenate single-omics tools rather than performing true integration, so the apparent abundance of platforms should not be mistaken for methodological diversity.

sections.heading: Network-based and deep learning approaches
sections.goal: Map the rapidly expanding family of methods that treat omics features as nodes in graphs or learn joint embeddings with neural architectures. Cover similarity-network fusion, graph neural networks, attention and transformer models, and CNN-based image-style integration. The critical angle: these methods report strong classification metrics but often on a narrow panel of cancer datasets, lack interpretability benchmarks, and rarely expose uncertainty — a defect that 'trustworthy' frameworks such as TMODINET only partially address.

sections.heading: Data structures, workflow systems and reproducibility
sections.goal: Evaluate the scaffolding on which analysis runs: Bioconductor's MultiAssayExperiment and SummarizedExperiment classes, workflow managers (Nextflow, Snakemake), containerisation, FAIR Digital Objects, simulation engines and pipeline-wrapping tools. The critical angle: reproducibility is repeatedly declared solved by the next containerised workflow, yet studies routinely skip metadata standards, version pinning, and provenance for derived layers; reproducibility should be measured by re-execution success on independent infrastructure, not by the mere presence of a Dockerfile.

sections.heading: Benchmarking evidence and evaluation criteria
sections.goal: Distil what the existing benchmarking literature actually establishes and what it does not. Highlight single-cell benchmarks (Hu et al.; Xiao et al.) and pan-cancer method comparisons (Ren et al.; Zhao et al.). The critical angle: most benchmarks use TCGA cancer data, evaluate only a handful of cancer-subtyping tasks, and rarely assess calibration, uncertainty, robustness to missingness, or biological interpretability; transferability of rankings to microbiome, single-cell or longitudinal settings is largely unproven.

sections.heading: EasyMultiProfiler: design, strengths and limitations relative to the alternatives
sections.goal: Dedicated, balanced assessment of EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) using the same criteria applied elsewhere: integration strategy, data structures, benchmarking evidence, scope and reproducibility. The critical angle: EMP's distinguishing choices — SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment back-end, a natural-language pipeline syntax spanning extraction to visualisation, and a clear focus on host–microbiome integration — are genuine advantages over generic Bioconductor or web platforms, yet the published evidence base is concentrated on human/mouse gut datasets, statistical benchmarking is limited and documentation of uncertainty quantification, deep-learning options and large-scale cloud execution is modest; EMP should be regarded as an excellent microbiome workflow rather than a universal integration engine.

sections.heading: Critical perspectives, controversies, recommendations and roadmap
sections.goal: Synthesise the recurring controversies — reproducibility, annotation dependence, interpretability, transferability across organisms — and translate the comparison into actionable guidance for users and developers. The critical angle: the field's centre of gravity has shifted from statistical novelty to infrastructure (workflows, data classes, FAIR packaging), but microbiome-specific tools remain under-benchmarked; recommend layered adoption (data class first, method second, platform last) and call for open benchmarks on shared microbiome multi-omics cohorts with explicit missingness, batch and strain-level stress tests.
